content: A citrate is the ionic form of citric acid, represented chemically as C3H5O(COO)33−. This structure is essentially citric acid with three hydrogen ions removed. Citrates are a family of compounds that include both ionic salts and covalent esters. For example, sodium citrate is a salt, while trimethyl citrate is an ester. There are many other compounds in this category. Citric acid, being a multifunctional acid, can also exist in intermediate ionic forms. These include the hydrogen citrate ion (HC6H5O72−) and the dihydrogen citrate ion (H2C6H5O7−). These intermediate ions can also form salts, which are referred to as acid salts. The pH characteristics of citrate salts depend on the specific ion involved. Salts of hydrogen citrate ions are weakly acidic, whereas salts of the citrate ion itself, when paired with an inert cation like sodium, are weakly basic. Citrate plays a significant role in buffering systems. It is a key component of the SSC 20X hybridization buffer, which is commonly used in molecular biology. However, there is a common error in the preparation of this buffer as described in some authoritative literature (e.g., Maniatis). The instructions suggest mixing 3M NaCl and 0.3M sodium citrate and then titrating the solution to a pH of 7 using NaOH. In reality, when these components are mixed, the resulting solution is slightly basic. Therefore, the pH should be adjusted downward to 7 using HCl instead. Additionally, citric acid can function as a mild chelating agent. In metabolism, citrate is a critical intermediate in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, also known as the Krebs cycle. After pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (which requires five cofactors: thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoamide, FAD, NAD+, and CoA), citrate synthase catalyzes the reaction between oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA to produce citrate. Citrate then progresses through the TCA cycle, undergoing transformations via enzymes like aconitase, eventually regenerating oxaloacetate. This regenerated oxaloacetate can then combine with another acetyl-CoA molecule to continue the cycle. Citrate also plays a regulatory role in glycolysis. When present in high concentrations, citrate can inhibit the enzyme phosphofructokinase, which is a key regulatory enzyme and the rate-limiting step of glycolysis. This inhibition serves as a feedback mechanism to regulate energy production in the cell.
